The model predicts you have a 51% chance of failing your final year, which means the system sees enough risk that you are required to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, almost none had any prior failures, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you to fail again. 

Two other factors pulled in the opposite direction. You report having very low free time after school, which the model sees as a positive signal because students who pass also tend to have limited unstructured time, possibly because they are focused on their work. Similarly, you described your family relationships as good, and this also nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, since strong family support often helps students succeed.

Even with these encouraging elements, your past academic setback outweighed them, tipping the overall prediction just above the failure threshold. To improve, you should treat this as an early warning: focus on consistent study habits, use your family support to create a realistic revision plan, and address any gaps from that earlier failure before they grow. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a smart first step toward changing the outcome. (218 words)
